kurals.tamil:
புல்லா திராஅப் புலத்தை அவர்உறும்
அல்லல்நோய் காண்கம் சிறிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Pullaa thiraaap pulaththai avar-urum
allalnoai kaankam siridhu.
kurals.meaning: Hold back your embrace and sulk a little, so that we may watch for a short while the ache of love he suffers.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend comes home very late after promising to be early. Your sister whispers, ‘Pretend to be a tiny bit upset for a minute, so he sees how much he was missed.’ It is a small, gentle game, not real anger, and it only lasts a moment.
kurals.university: The chapter on pulavi (a lovers’ sulk within married love, kaṟpu) opens with the speaker, read as the confidante (tōḻi), urging the wife: pullātu irā (‘remain without embracing’) and pulattai (‘sulk’), so that ‘we’ may see (kāṇkam) for a little (ciṟitu) the allal nōy (‘anguished love-sickness’) he will feel. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all gloss it this way, the first-person plural binding the confidante to the wife’s side, and Pope’s verse likewise asks her to stay reserved and decline his proffered love so as to prove his distress a little while. The limiting word ciṟitu anticipates the next couplet’s warning that the sulk must not be prolonged. ytamizh.com prints அவர்உறும் where thirukkural.net prints the joined form அவருறும், a difference of word division only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna, wishing to see his queen Rukmini’s face in loving pique, teases her by suggesting she would have done better to marry a king of her own rank; she is so stricken that she faints, and he at once lifts her up and consoles her.
hinduism.explanation: The god himself plays a brief game of provocation to see how deeply his beloved feels, then ends it quickly with tenderness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s confidante proposes the same short test from the other side: hold back a little and see how much he cares.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a good match on a deliberate, brief test of a lover’s feeling, though here the husband provokes the wife rather than the reverse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
christianity.explanation: The bride is slow to open the door to her beloved, and by the time she does he has gone, leaving her searching in distress.
christianity.tie_back: The Song shows how a moment of holding back makes the lover’s absence felt sharply, which is the effect the Kural’s confidante wants to produce in the husband.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a partial match, since the bride’s delay is not a planned test and the pain falls on her rather than on him.

islam.quote_or_event: In his treatise on love, Ibn Hazm describes a kind of ‘breaking off’ (hajr) that lovers adopt playfully, out of coquetry, and says that such feigned avoidance can be sweeter than many a meeting.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar treats mock coldness between lovers as part of love’s pleasure rather than a real rupture.
islam.tie_back: The confidante’s advice is exactly this kind of playful, temporary coldness meant to be enjoyed rather than to wound.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on Breaking Off (paraphrase; tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the chapter on hajr, not verified against a live text this session; a close thematic match, though it is Andalusian love literature rather than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: When his brothers come to Egypt, Joseph hides who he is, speaks roughly to them and tests them, turning aside to weep in private before he finally reveals himself.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s concealment lets him see how his brothers really feel, though it costs him tears of his own.
judaism.tie_back: Like the sulking wife, Joseph holds back his embrace for a little while to see the other side’s heart, then ends the test in reunion.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous narrative; the structure of withheld embrace and testing matches, but the context is family reconciliation, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada warns that those who keep thinking ‘he abused me, he wronged me’ never quiet their resentment, while those who let such thoughts go find peace.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism treats dwelling on a grievance, even a small one, as something that feeds suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural enjoys a little staged grievance; the Dhammapada would gently caution that even play-resentment should be dropped quickly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Buddhist teaching runs against the Kural’s playful sulking, though it shares the concern that grievance be brief.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra teaches that all beings are fond of life, like pleasure and hate pain, so a mendicant should cause pain to none.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics extends non-harm (ahimsa) even to the small pains we cause others in thought and word.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural takes playful pleasure in a lover’s brief distress, which Jain teaching on non-harm would treat with caution rather than delight.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra 1.2.3 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Jainism does not celebrate the lovers’ game, so this is a contrasting parallel; paraphrased, not verified verbatim this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope will not run to embrace him; she holds back and tests him by ordering their bed moved, and only when he protests that it cannot be moved does she weep and embrace him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s cool reserve draws out a burst of feeling from her husband that proves who he is.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Penelope withholds her embrace for a little while and watches his distress before yielding.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a strong match on deliberate holding back from a returning husband, though Penelope’s motive is caution, not a lovers’ game.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that absence lessens moderate passions and increases great ones, as the wind puts out candles but fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: A little distance, he suggests, reveals how strong a love really is.
philosophy.tie_back: The confidante’s plan rests on the same insight: a brief coldness will show, and even heighten, how much he loves.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim; a reasonable match on distance testing love, though it concerns absence rather than a deliberate sulk.

kurals.tamil:
உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி அதுசிறிது
மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uppamain thatraal pulavi adhusiridhu
mikkatraal neela vidal.
kurals.meaning: A lovers’ sulk is like salt in the right measure; to let it run on too long is like putting in a little too much salt.
kurals.elementary: A pinch of salt makes soup taste wonderful, but too much salt spoils it. A small, short sulk between people who love each other is like that pinch; a long one ruins everything.
kurals.university: The famous image here is culinary: pulavi is uppu amaintaṟṟu (‘like salt properly set’ in food), but to let it lengthen (nīḷa viṭal) is like salt that has become a little excessive (atu ciṟitu mikkaṟṟu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read ciṟitu with mikku (‘even slightly too much’), stressing how quickly the right measure is lost, while Kalaignar reads the measure as the interval between quarrel (ūṭal) and reunion (kūṭal), and Solomon Pappaiah relates it to the joy of union it is meant to season. The couplet is generally taken as the confidante’s counsel to the wife, balancing the previous verse’s encouragement. Pope renders ‘A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess, / Too long maintained, ’tis like the salt’s excess.’ ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend urges her not to keep up her proud anger (mana) against Krishna, who has come to her humbly, warning her that by being harsh to one so gentle she only hurts herself.
hinduism.explanation: The sakhi plays exactly the Kural confidante’s role, telling the heroine that her pique has gone on long enough.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the salt warning in Sanskrit lyric form: a little pique adds savour, but prolonged pride spoils the love it was meant to season.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Sarga 9 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of the canto in which the friend rebukes Radha’s prolonged mana; a close match in situation and speaker, not verified verbatim this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger may arise but insists it must not be carried past the end of the day.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural accepts a little sulking but, like Paul, sets a firm limit on how long it may last.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on keeping anger short, though Paul speaks of community life generally, not lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is not lawful for a man to desert his brother Muslim for more than three nights. (It is unlawful for them that) when they meet, one of them turns his face away from the other, and the other turns his face from the former, and the better of the two will be the one who greets the other first.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet sets a strict time limit on estrangement and praises whoever ends it first.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s salt image makes the same point: a short coolness is tolerable, a prolonged one corrupts the relationship.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a strong match on limiting the length of estrangement, though it concerns fellow believers rather than spouses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes divine anger as brief and divine favour as lasting.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural wants love’s anger in the same proportion: a moment of sulk inside a lifetime of affection.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a real parallel on anger kept brief, though the psalm speaks of God, not lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the monk Sona strains too hard in his practice, the Buddha reminds him that a lute is neither in tune nor playable when its strings are too tight or too slack, but only when they are evenly tuned.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches balance: too much or too little effort both spoil the practice.
buddhism.tie_back: The lute string and the Kural’s salt teach the same lesson of right measure, applied here to a lovers’ sulk.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile; a good structural match on measure, though the subject is meditative effort, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names anger (krodha) and pride (mana) as passions that eat away at relationships.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural warns that a sulk kept up too long, like over-salting, destroys the affection it was meant to spice.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse, not verified verbatim this session and verse numbering varies; a good match on anger and pride eroding love, though Jainism wants these passions removed, not measured.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Angered over the loss of Briseis, Achilles withdraws to his tent and refuses even the generous amends Agamemnon’s envoys bring, prolonging his wrath until it costs the life of his dearest friend Patroclus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles’ wrath, held too long, turns from a just grievance into a disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s too-much-salt in epic form: a grievance nursed beyond its measure ruins what it was meant to defend.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the central plot of the Iliad; a good match on a sulk prolonged to ruin, though it is a warrior’s wrath, not a lovers’ pout.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle places good temper at the mean in anger and describes ‘sulky’ people as hard to appease, holding their anger a long time.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the virtuous person feels anger at the right things, toward the right people, and for the right length of time.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s salt is Aristotle’s mean in the kitchen: the right amount of sulk at the right moment, and not a moment longer.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Aristotle’s discussion of good temper; a strong match on the right duration of anger, though not specific to lovers.

kurals.tamil:
அலந்தாரை அல்லல்நோய் செய்தற்றால் தம்மைப்
புலந்தாரைப் புல்லா விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Alandhaarai allalnoai seydhatraal thammaip
pulandhaaraip pullaa vidal.
kurals.meaning: Not to embrace and reconcile the one who sulks with you is like heaping fresh pain on someone who is already suffering.
kurals.elementary: If your little sister is sad and pretending not to talk to you, and you just walk away, she feels even worse than before. A hug at the right moment is what she was secretly waiting for.
kurals.university: The address now turns to the husband: to leave unembraced (pullā viṭal) those who have sulked with him (tammaip pulantār) is like inflicting allal nōy (‘anguish, sickness’) on alantār, ‘those already distressed.’ Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘not dispelling the sulk and embracing’ (ūṭal uṇarttit taḻuvāmal), Solomon Pappaiah names the wife explicitly, and Puliyur Kesikan calls such neglect a cruelty; the point is that the sulk is itself a symptom of the pain of separation, so ignoring it compounds that pain. Pope’s explanation reads ‘For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony.’ The two web texts agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha in her anger and pleads with her at length, begging her to give up her pique, offering himself to any punishment she chooses, and asking her to place her foot on his head as a sign of forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: The divine lover does not leave his beloved to her sulk; he humbles himself to end it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the response the Kural asks of the husband: go to the one who sulks and reconcile, rather than adding to her pain.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Sarga 10 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known canto of Krishna’s appeasement; a close match in situation, not verified verbatim this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb lists actions that make a bad situation worse for someone already hurting.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural also uses a comparison to show that ignoring a hurting partner adds pain to pain.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good structural match on compounding another’s distress, though not about lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an urges spouses who drift apart to seek reconciliation, declaring that settlement is best.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise tells the husband that the right response to his wife’s withdrawal is to make peace, not to leave her alone.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a real parallel on marital reconciliation, though it concerns serious estrangement rather than playful sulking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rav says: A person must always be careful about mistreatment of his wife. Since her tear is easily elicited, punishment for her mistreatment is immediate.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud warns husbands that a wife’s hurt is close to the surface and wronging her carries quick consequences.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural gives the husband the same warning: his sulking wife is already in pain, and neglect only deepens it.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Koren-Steinsaltz English, including its explanatory insertion); a strong match on not adding to a wife’s hurt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Finding a monk lying sick and neglected in his own filth, the Buddha and Ananda wash and tend him, and the Buddha tells the monks that whoever would tend him should tend the sick.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha makes caring for the suffering a duty and rebukes those who leave a sufferer alone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly condemns leaving someone already in distress without the comfort they need.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the principle of not abandoning the suffering matches, but the setting is monastic care, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra names four attitudes to cultivate: friendliness toward all beings, joy at the virtuous, compassion (karunya) toward the afflicted, and equanimity toward the ill-behaved.
jainism.explanation: Compassion toward those already suffering is a core Jain disposition.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband is asked for exactly this compassion toward a partner whose sulk is itself a form of suffering.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (Digambara numbering; 7.6 in the Svetambara recension) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard sutra; a fair match on compassion for the afflicted, though Jainism frames it as a spiritual discipline, not marital tenderness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Once Penelope has tested and recognized Odysseus, she runs to him in tears and embraces him, and he holds her weeping, the reunion as welcome as land to shipwrecked swimmers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The long estrangement and testing end in an embrace that heals both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural insists that a sulk must end in such an embrace, since withholding it would only prolong pain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a good match on reconciliation by embrace, though the preceding coldness is not a lovers’ pout.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch praises the Pythagoreans who, whenever anger led them to harsh words, would join right hands and embrace before the sun went down and be reconciled.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch holds up quick, physical reconciliation as the mark of people bound by real affection.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks the husband for the same prompt embrace that ends a quarrel before it hardens.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, On Brotherly Love (De fraterno amore), Moralia (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified this session; a good match on reconciliation by embrace, though about brothers and fellow philosophers.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடி யவரை உணராமை வாடிய
வள்ளி முதலரிந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Ooti yavarai unaraamai vaatiya
valli mudhalarin thatru.
kurals.meaning: Failing to soothe and win back the one who sulks is like cutting at the root a creeper that is already wilting.
kurals.elementary: A thirsty plant droops when it needs water. If, instead of watering it, someone cut its root, it would never recover. Someone who is sulking is like that drooping plant: they need care, not to be ignored.
kurals.university: Ūṭiyavarai uṇarāmai, ‘not making those who sulk understand (and so ending the sulk),’ is likened to cutting at the root (mutal arital) a valli creeper that is already wilted (vāṭiya). Uṇartal here is the technical term for appeasing a lover’s sulk by explanation and tenderness; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss ‘without showing love,’ while Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah add that the creeper had already withered for want of water, so the cutting destroys any chance of recovery. The image completes the previous couplet: the sulk is a sign of a love already parched by separation, and neglect kills it outright. Pope renders the explanation ‘Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root.’ The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Where the female relations live in grief, the family soon wholly perishes; but that family where they are not unhappy ever prospers.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu tie the survival of a household to the contentment of its women.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s withering creeper is the same warning in a single image: a grieving partner left uncomforted means the family’s love dies at the root.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Bühler); a strong match on a household withering when its women grieve, though Manu speaks of female relations generally, not a wife’s sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.”
christianity.explanation: Matthew applies Isaiah’s prophecy to Jesus, who does not crush what is already weak and fading.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s plant image says the same: what is already drooping should be restored, not cut down.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match in image (a weakened plant not to be destroyed), though the context is messianic gentleness, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes marriage as a bond meant to be sustained by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: Neglecting a sulking partner withholds the very mercy that keeps this bond alive, as the Kural’s cut creeper shows.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a general match on mercy sustaining marriage, without the Kural’s specific image of neglect.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, And bring her into the wilderness, And speak tenderly unto her.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea pictures God, the estranged husband of Israel, winning back his alienated bride with tender words rather than abandoning her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks the husband to do the same: woo back the one who has withdrawn instead of letting the bond wither.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on tender appeasement of an estranged beloved, though Hosea’s marriage is an allegory of God and Israel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the monks of Kosambi quarrel bitterly, the Buddha urges them to reconcile and teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred, but only by non-hatred.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats lingering estrangement as something that destroys community unless met with goodwill.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that a quarrel left unhealed destroys the relationship at its root.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode and verse; a fair match on healing estrangement, though monastic rather than marital.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Prince Pavananjaya, stung by a slight on his wedding day, neglects his wife Anjana for years while she pines; on campaign he sees a chakravaka bird crying for its lost mate, realizes his cruelty, and hurries back to her.
jainism.explanation: The story shows a husband who nearly destroys his marriage through stubborn neglect and is brought back by an image of grieving love.
jainism.tie_back: Pavananjaya’s neglect of the pining Anjana is the Kural’s withered creeper cut at the root, narrowly averted.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Anjana-Pavananjaya episode; paraphrase; also in Hemacandra’s Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, book 7)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain narrative from memory, not verified verbatim this session; a strong match on neglect of a sulking or pining spouse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Echo, rejected by Narcissus, wastes away in grief until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows love that is spurned withering until nothing of the lover is left.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wilting creeper cut at the root is the same fate: love ignored does not survive.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous myth; a good match on love withering under neglect, though Echo and Narcissus were never a couple.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle quotes the saying that lack of conversation has broken many a friendship, noting that friends who do not meet and share their lives let affection fade.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, even good friendships need active upkeep or they die away.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same about love: if the sulking partner is not drawn back, the bond withers at its root.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a good match on neglect ending affection, though about friendship rather than marriage.

kurals.tamil:
நலத்தகை நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் புலத்தகை
பூஅன்ன கண்ணார் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nalaththakai nallavarkku aeer pulaththakai
pooanna kannaar akaththu.
kurals.meaning: Even for good men of fine character, the real ornament is the loving pique that rises in the hearts of their flower-eyed wives.
kurals.elementary: A kind, good person is like a fine house. What makes the house feel truly loved is that someone inside cares enough to be a little upset when you are late. That small fuss is a sign of how much you matter.
kurals.university: Nalattakai nallavar are ‘good men of excellent quality’; their ēr (‘beauty, ornament’) is the pulattakai (‘the excellence of sulking’) that arises akattu (‘within,’ in the heart) of pū aṉṉa kaṇṇār, ‘those with flower-like eyes.’ The paradox is that the husband’s virtues are crowned not by praise but by his beloved’s pique, which proves her attachment; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it this way, Solomon Pappaiah speaks of the abundance of sulking in the wife’s mind, and Kalaignar says such pique ‘adds beauty’ to noble lovers. Pope translates ‘Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulance / Of wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace.’ ytamizh.com divides நல்லவர்க்கு ஏஎர் and பூஅன்ன, while thirukkural.net prints the sandhi forms நல்லவர்க் கேஎர் and பூவன்ன.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Harivamsa, Satyabhama, roused to jealousy when Krishna gives a celestial flower to Rukmini, retires in sulking anger, and Krishna, the ideal husband, appeases her by promising to bring her the whole Parijata tree from heaven.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna’s greatness is displayed precisely in how he honours and answers his queen’s pique.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, a good man’s glory is shown in the loving pique of his wife and in his response to it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely retold episode whose details vary between versions; not verified verbatim this session, and the fit is thematic rather than exact.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.”
christianity.explanation: The epistle tells husbands to live with understanding and to honour their wives as co-heirs.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise measures a good husband by how he receives his wife’s feelings, including her pique.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a loose match on a husband’s honour toward his wife, with nothing on pique as an ornament.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that the best of people are those who are best to their families, and that he was the best of them to his own family.
islam.explanation: A man’s true excellence is measured inside his home, by how he treats his wife.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly locates a good man’s real beauty in his relationship with his wife and her feelings toward him.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, not verified verbatim this session; a fair match on a man’s worth shown in his home, without the Kural’s focus on pique.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, With one bead of thy necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover is overcome by a single glance of his bride’s eyes.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too gives the power to the beloved’s eyes, likened to flowers, whose moods shape her husband’s happiness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a partial match on the beloved’s eyes ruling the lover’s heart, without the theme of pique.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha teaches that a husband should minister to his wife by honouring her, not disparaging her, being faithful, handing over authority in the home and providing her with adornments.
buddhism.explanation: A good layman’s virtue is shown in how respectfully he treats his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural locates a good man’s ornament in his wife’s feelings; the sutta shows the respect that makes such loving pique safe to express.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard sutta; a general match on a husband’s duties, but nothing on pique as an adornment.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tamil Jain epic Jivaka Chintamani follows its hero through a series of courtships and marriages, portraying each bride’s feelings with care before Jivaka finally renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: Jain literature can depict married love vividly, though it treats it as a stage on the way to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates a wife’s pique as a husband’s ornament, a valuation Jain narrative would admire as poetry but not as a final goal.
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a general reference to a Tamil Jain romance epic, not a specific verse, and Jain doctrine does not prize lovers’ pique.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the walls of Troy, Andromache reproaches Hector for his recklessness in battle and pleads with him to stay; he answers her tenderly, holding their son and comforting her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector’s nobility shines most clearly in the scene where his wife scolds him out of love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the hero’s best ornament is the loving reproach of his wife and his gentle reply.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a fair match on a wife’s loving reproach honouring her husband, though her fear is for his life, not a lovers’ pout.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence has a character remark that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love.
philosophy.explanation: The Roman playwright turns lovers’ anger into a sign of love’s vitality.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a wife’s pique as something that adorns, rather than diminishes, a good man’s love.
philosophy.source: Terence, Andria, Act III, sc. 3 (amantium irae amoris integratio est; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous Latin line from comedy rather than philosophy proper; a reasonable match on lovers’ quarrels as a good sign.

kurals.tamil:
துனியும் புலவியும் இல்லாயின் காமம்
கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuniyum pulaviyum illaayin kaamam
kaniyum karukkaayum atru.
kurals.meaning: Love without its deeper quarrels and its small sulks is like fruit that is either over-ripe or still hard and green.
kurals.elementary: A mango that is too soft and mushy is no good, and one that is still hard and green is no good either. Love that never has a single little disagreement is a bit like that: it has lost its just-right sweetness.
kurals.university: Two grades of lovers’ anger are named: tuṉi, the grown or deep sulk, and pulavi, the young or light sulk, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses them (vaḷarnta ūṭal and iḷam ūṭal); without them kāmam is like kaṉi (fruit gone too ripe) and karukkāy (fruit not yet ripe). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read both fruits as useless, the over-ripe one past its best and the unripe one inedible, while Kalaignar adds ‘rotten’ to the over-ripe fruit; some readers pair the two terms with the two fruits, but the commentators quoted take the comparison as a whole. Pope’s couplet, ‘Love without hatred is ripened fruit; / Without some lesser strife, fruit immature,’ makes that pairing explicit. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A much-quoted verse of Sanskrit poetics holds that love in union does not reach its fullness without love in separation, just as a cloth first treated with astringent takes a deeper dye.
hinduism.explanation: Indian aesthetic theory treats separation and pique (vipralambha, including mana) as what gives union its depth of flavour.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ripe-fruit image makes the same claim: without its quarrels, love lacks its full savour.
hinduism.source: Verse on śṛṅgāra cited in alaṅkāra works such as Viśvanātha’s Sāhityadarpaṇa (paraphrase; attribution not verified)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse whose exact locus was not verified this session; a close thematic match on separation and pique deepening love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews teaches that what is painful at the moment can ripen into good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise sees love’s small pains as part of how it ripens.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); only a loose match through the image of pain yielding fruit, since Hebrews speaks of divine discipline.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an twice declares that with hardship comes ease.
islam.explanation: Difficulty and relief are presented as bound together in the divine order of things.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats the friction of sulking as inseparable from love’s sweetness.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very familiar verse; next-best only, since it concerns life’s trials generally, not lovers’ quarrels.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes sees both embracing and holding back as part of life’s proper seasons.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too gives holding back a place within love, without which love would lose its right ripeness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a good match on a season for refraining from embrace, though Ecclesiastes does not value it as love’s seasoning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that attachment to the beloved brings pain, and advises freedom from both liking and disliking.
buddhism.tie_back: Where the Kural welcomes love’s little pains as part of its sweetness, the Dhammapada sees them as a reason to loosen attachment altogether.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; included as a contrasting view, since Buddhism does not prize love’s quarrels.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain karma theory grades each passion, such as anger (krodha) and pride (mana), by intensity and duration, from the most binding kind that can last a lifetime down to the mildest, flickering kind that passes in about a fortnight.
jainism.explanation: Jainism carefully distinguishes deep from light passions, but treats all of them as binding karma to be overcome.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also distinguishes a deep sulk (tuni) from a light one (pulavi), though it values both where Jainism would seek to remove them.
jainism.source: Jain doctrine of the four grades of kashaya (e.g. Karmagrantha; summarized in P.S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard doctrine from a secondary summary, not verified this session; the grading parallels the Kural, but the valuation is opposite.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros glukupikron, ‘sweet-bitter,’ a creature that cannot be fought off.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Sappho love is by nature a mixture of sweetness and pain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural agrees that love without its bitter edge is not fully ripe.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho, fragment 130 (paraphrase; cf. tr. D.A. Campbell, Greek Lyric I)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very short, famous fragment; a strong match on love’s mingled sweetness and bitterness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that hatred which is fully overcome by love passes into love, and that the love is then greater than if hatred had not come before it.
philosophy.explanation: On Spinoza’s account, a conflict overcome can leave affection stronger than before.
philosophy.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that love’s quarrels, once resolved, make it richer, like fruit brought to the right ripeness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a specific proposition, not verified verbatim this session; a strong match on conflict deepening love.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடலின் உண்டாங்கோர் துன்பம் புணர்வது
நீடுவ தன்றுகொல் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodalin untaangoar thunpam punarvadhu
needuva thandrukol endru.
kurals.meaning: Even in a lovers’ quarrel there is a kind of pain: the worry that their time together may not last long enough.
kurals.elementary: When you pretend to be cross with a friend during a sleepover, part of you worries, ‘What if this wastes our fun time together?’ The game is nice, but it also has a little worry inside it.
kurals.university: Ūṭalin uṇṭu āṅku ōr tuṉpam, ‘in sulking too there is a certain sorrow,’ namely the fear, puṇarvatu nīṭuvatu aṉṟu kol, ‘whether union will not last long.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read nīṭuvatu as ‘prolonging, lasting’: the lovers fear that time lost to sulking shortens their time together. Pope’s verse instead asks ‘Will reunion sweet be long delayed?’, reading the worry as delay of reconciliation rather than brevity of union, and his prose explanation follows the same line; both readings keep the paradox that the sulk, meant to heighten love, carries its own anxiety. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Cloud Messenger, an exiled yaksha, separated from his wife for a year, frets over whether she is surviving the separation and sends a cloud to reassure her that their reunion will come.
hinduism.explanation: The poem is a long meditation on the anxiety that separation may cut love short.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers feel a small version of the same fear: that their time apart, even in a sulk, might cost them their union.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s frame story; a fair match on anxiety for lost time together, though the separation is a curse, not a sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb names the sickness of waiting for what one longs for and the joy of finally receiving it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sulking lover feels exactly this ache of deferred union inside the game of pique.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on the pain of delayed fulfilment, though not specific to lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens his Masnavi with the reed flute, which tells its tale by complaining of separation from the reed-bed it was cut from.
islam.explanation: The reed’s lament is Sufism’s classic image of longing for reunion with the beloved.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s lover, even while sulking, feels the reed’s pang: the fear of being kept from the beloved.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1 ff. (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the famous opening; a fair match on the pain of separation, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved lies awake searching for the one she loves and cannot find him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover shares this anxious search for union, even when the separation is self-imposed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a good match on longing for a lost beloved, though no quarrel is involved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that loving attachment inevitably brings the fear of losing what one loves.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural observes this very fear inside love’s quarrel, though it accepts it as part of love rather than a reason to let go.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong match on fear born of love, with the opposite conclusion about attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Uttaradhyayana Sutra teaches that one who is attached to pleasing objects is never free from anxiety, suffering in getting them, in keeping them and in losing them.
jainism.explanation: For Jainism, attachment (raga) carries its own built-in worry about loss.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover experiences exactly this worry, fearing the loss of union even in the middle of a playful sulk.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the chapter’s teaching on attachment, not verified verbatim this session; a fair match on anxiety in love, with Jainism urging its removal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leading Eurydice up from the underworld, Orpheus, afraid she might be failing and eager to see her, looks back too soon and loses her forever.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s telling, the lover’s anxious fear of losing his beloved is what costs him their reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover carries a gentler form of the same fear, that union may slip away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous myth; a fair match on fear of losing union, though far more tragic than a lovers’ sulk.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal describes a ‘second crystallization’ in love, born when doubt arises about whether one is loved, and says this anxious phase makes love far stronger.
philosophy.explanation: Stendhal treats the lover’s fear of losing the beloved as both painful and intensifying.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly finds a sorrow in the lovers’ quarrel that comes from fear for the union itself.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour), Book I (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known idea; a good match on the anxiety within love, though Stendhal’s doubt is about being loved, not about lost time.

kurals.tamil:
நோதல் எவன்மற்று நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும்
காதலர் இல்லா வழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Noadhal evanmatru nondhaarendru aqdhariyum
kaadhalar illaa vazhi.
kurals.meaning: What use is it to grieve, when there is no lover who will understand, ‘This sorrow is because of me’?
kurals.elementary: If you sulk in your room, it only helps if someone who loves you notices and comes to ask what is wrong. If nobody notices at all, the sulking just makes you lonely.
kurals.university: Nōtal evaṉ maṟṟu, ‘what then is the use of grieving,’ when there are no kātalar, ‘lovers,’ who know it (aḵtu aṟiyum) as nontār eṉṟu, ‘she has grieved (because of us).’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the lover’s grief as worthwhile only when the beloved recognizes himself as its cause; Kesikan adds that such a lover would then try to remove it. The verse states the precondition of the whole pulavi convention: a sulk is a message, and it needs a receiver. Pope’s prose explanation, ‘What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow?’, puts the words in the husband’s mouth, whereas the Tamil commentators leave the speaker general. ytamizh.com prints நொந்தாரென்று அஃதறியும் and thirukkural.net the sandhi form நொந்தாரென் றஃதறியும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the gopis of Vraja pour out their grief at Krishna’s absence to his messenger Uddhava, addressing a passing bee and asking what use their longing is when the one who caused it has gone away to the city.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis feel their grief is wasted unless the beloved knows and answers it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural states the same complaint: sorrow means little when the beloved does not recognize that it is for him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known Bee Song episode, not verified verbatim this session; a good match on grief addressed to an absent lover.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share in one another’s feelings, so no one grieves alone.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same need: grief has meaning only when someone who loves us shares and understands it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a reasonable match on shared sorrow, though addressed to a community, not to lovers.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, grieving for Joseph, directs his complaint only to the One who truly knows and cares.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that grief should be addressed to one who will understand it; without such a listener, it is wasted.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a good match on grief needing a knowing listener, though Jacob addresses God, not a lover.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look on my right hand, and see, For there is no man that knoweth me; I have no way to flee; No man careth for my soul.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist laments that no one recognizes him or cares about his distress.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s situation exactly: sorrow with no one who knows it is for them, and so no one to answer it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on grief with no one who knows or cares, though the psalm is not about love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that one does not gain peace by weeping and lamenting; grieving only increases one’s pain and harms the body, and does nothing for the one mourned.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism sees lamentation as useless suffering that should be pulled out like an arrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also asks what grief accomplishes, though it answers that it helps only when a loving partner recognizes it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta on grief, not verified verbatim this session; a partial match on the futility of grief, with a different conclusion.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Prince Neminatha turns back from his own wedding and renounces the world, his bride Rajimati grieves for the one who has left her, then follows him into the ascetic life.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s grief has no one to answer it, so she transforms it into renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural asks what grief is for when the beloved will not acknowledge it; Rajimati’s answer is to let it lead beyond worldly love.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Rathanemi chapter’s narrative, not verified verbatim this session; a fair match on grief without a responding lover, with a Jain resolution.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Abandoned by Theseus on the shore of Naxos, Ariadne pours out her lament to the empty sea and the winds, with no one to hear her complaint.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her grief is all the more bitter because the one who caused it is gone and cannot hear it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s grief without a knowing lover is exactly Ariadne’s situation on the deserted shore.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous lament; a strong match on grief with no lover to receive it, though Ariadne has been truly abandoned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon writes that friendship doubles joys and cuts griefs in half, since no one shares a sorrow with a friend without grieving the less.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon sees grief as lightened only when another person receives it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s question rests on the same insight: sorrow has its use only when someone who loves us understands it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous essay; a good match on grief needing a sharer, though about friends rather than lovers.

kurals.tamil:
நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே புலவியும்
வீழுநர் கண்ணே இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Neerum nizhaladhu inidhae pulaviyum
veezhunar kannae inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Water is sweet only when it lies in the shade; sulking too is sweet only with those who truly love.
kurals.elementary: Water in a sunny puddle gets hot and yucky, but water in a cool shady pond tastes lovely. A little sulk is only nice between people who love each other; with someone who does not care, it is just unpleasant.
kurals.university: Nīrum niḻalatu iṉitē, ‘even water is sweet only when in the shade,’ and pulaviyum vīḻunar kaṇṇē iṉitu, ‘sulking too is sweet only with (vīḻunar) those who desire/love.’ The emphatic -ē particles stress exclusivity: pique has its charm only inside a secure, mutual love. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss vīḻunar as those who show love; Solomon Pappaiah contrasts water under the sun with water under the shade; Kalaignar notes that water by the shade is cool. Pope renders ‘Water is pleasant in the cooling shade; / So coolness for a time with those we love.’ ytamizh.com divides நிழலது இனிதே, while thirukkural.net prints the metrical division நிழல தினிதே, the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Please tolerate the wrongs that I may have done to You and bear with me as a father with his son, or a friend with his friend, or a lover with his beloved.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna appeals to the special forbearance that exists within loving relationships.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that friction is sweet only within such relationships, where love bears it gladly.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 11.44 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a good match on love making offences bearable, though Arjuna is asking pardon of God.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb holds that hurt from someone who truly loves you is trustworthy, while sweetness from an enemy is not.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that a sulk is sweet only from those who love; its value depends on the love behind it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on hurt being acceptable only within love, though about friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.” … “When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Thereupon I said, “Yes (you are right), but by Allah, O Allah’s Messenger, I leave nothing but your name.”
islam.explanation: Aisha’s sulks with the Prophet are gentle and affectionate: even when cross she leaves out only his name, never him.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sweet pique between those who love, where the anger is only skin deep and the love remains whole.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com (ellipsis marks omitted words; the honorific is abbreviated); a close match on affectionate pique within a loving marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For whom the LORD loveth He correcteth, Even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.”
judaism.explanation: Correction is presented as a sign of love, not of rejection.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly treats a sulk as sweet because it comes from love; between strangers it would be only bitter.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a partial match on displeasure as a sign of love, framed as divine discipline.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: Reproof from the right person, a wise friend, is welcomed as treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too says a reproach is sweet when it comes from the right person, one who loves.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a fair match on reproach valued by its source, though the Dhammapada speaks of wise teachers, not lovers.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Quitting your former connections place your affection on nothing; a monk who loves not even those who love him, will be freed from sin and hatred.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses tell the monk to give up affection even for those who love him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds sweetness in pique only among those who love; Jain monastic teaching would set aside even that loving bond.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting parallel only, since the verse renounces the very love the Kural celebrates.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls on Aphrodite, who comes down smiling and gently asks what troubles her this time and whom she should persuade to love her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess meets Sappho’s complaint with amused tenderness rather than annoyance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Complaint received with such loving indulgence is the Kural’s sweet pique: it is pleasant only where love already exists.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous poem; a partial match on complaint welcomed within love, though the relationship is goddess and devotee.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that the true friend is known by his frank speech, which stings but heals, while the flatterer only pleases.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, sharpness is welcome when it comes from genuine goodwill.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says a lover’s sharpness is sweet only because it comes from real love.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend, Moralia (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the essay’s main argument; a fair match on sharpness valued within goodwill, though about friendship, not love.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடல் உணங்க விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம்
கூடுவேம் என்பது அவா.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodal unanga viduvaaroadu en-nenjam
kooduvaem enpadhu avaa.
kurals.meaning: That my heart still says ‘let us be with him’ about one who leaves my sulk to wither unsoothed is nothing but sheer desire.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a friend does not even notice you are upset, and yet you still want to play with them. Your heart just wants to be with them anyway. That is how strong caring can be.
kurals.university: Ūṭal uṇaṅka viṭuvār, ‘one who leaves (my) sulk to dry up and wither’ (uṇaṅku, ‘to wither, dry’), without soothing it; that my heart (eṉ neñcam) still says kūṭuvēm, ‘we shall unite,’ with such a person is avā, ‘longing, desire.’ Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read the wife as speaker, explaining her heart’s persistence as untameable desire, which links the chapter to the preceding one on quarrelling with one’s own heart. Pope’s verse, ‘Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing,’ and his prose explanation take the husband as speaker; the Tamil itself leaves the gender open. ytamizh.com prints விடுவாரோடு என்நெஞ்சம் … என்பது அவா, and thirukkural.net the sandhi forms விடுவாரோ டென்னெஞ்சம் … என்ப தவா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Blessed Lord said: It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material modes of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring, sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked what drives a person against their own will, Krishna names desire (kama) as the force behind it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker reaches the same diagnosis: what drives her heart toward one who neglects her is nothing but desire.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a good match on desire overriding judgment, though the Gita condemns it while the Kural merely names it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as enduring every slight and still hoping.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heart shows this endurance, still seeking union with one who has left its sulk unsoothed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a fair match on love that persists despite neglect, though Paul praises it while the Kural half-rebukes it as mere desire.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun goes on longing for Layla through every obstacle and rejection, unable to turn his heart away even when union is impossible.
islam.explanation: Majnun’s love has become a desire beyond reason or reward.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker recognizes the same helpless longing in her own heart, which seeks union despite being neglected.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous romance; a fair match on unreasoning, persistent desire, though Majnun’s situation is far more extreme.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song declares that love cannot be put out by any obstacle.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart proves the point: not even the beloved’s neglect can quench its longing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a good match on love’s unquenchable persistence, though the Song celebrates it while the Kural sighs at it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From craving springs grief, from craving springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha identifies craving (tanha) as the root of the grief that comes with love.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker names her heart’s pull as avā, desire, the very craving the Dhammapada says breeds sorrow.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a good match on desire as the root of the trouble, though Buddhism counsels letting it go.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses describe desire as something that only grows as it is fed.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker sees the same restless desire in her heart, which keeps seeking union even with one who neglects her.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair match on insatiable desire, though the verse concerns greed rather than love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Dido writes to Aeneas as he prepares to abandon her, reproaching him yet still unable to stop loving him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Dido’s letter mixes complaint with a desire she cannot master.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker also still longs for one who leaves her hurt unsoothed, and calls it simply desire.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known poem; a fair match on love persisting despite neglect, though Dido’s case is tragic abandonment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, and can never by itself oppose a passion in directing the will.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, desire, not reason, ultimately moves us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker discovers the same thing: her judgment says the neglectful one deserves no union, but desire alone drives her heart.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous claim; a good match on desire overruling reason, though Hume states it as a general theory of action.
